symptom: a soft bulge on one side of the neck that puffs up with hard blowing
hook: A ping-pong ball of trapped air tucked beside the windpipe.
whatYouSee: A round black air-filled sac bulging out beside the larynx on the right side of the patient's neck.
whyItMatters: A laryngocele is an air-filled dilatation of the saccule of the laryngeal ventricle and can be internal, external, or mixed. It classically grows on straining such as in glass blowers or trumpet players.
treatment: If the swelling is confirmed on CT the treatment is surgical excision.
takeaway: An air-filled neck swelling that grows when the patient blows or strains points to a laryngocele.

defects: Unexplained additional image findings: ["The large air-filled sac is located on the patient's LEFT side (image right) rather than the expected RIGHT side (image left); however, since laterality is determined by the clinical description and no lead marker is present, this could represent a left-sided laryngocele — but the expected key finding specifically requires a right-sided lesion, making this a mismatch rather than an unexplained additional lesion","The air-filled sac appears to be at a slightly higher level (C3-C5) than the expected thyroid cartilage/thyrohyoid membrane level, sitting more superiorly in the neck"]

findings: AP projection of the cervical spine and upper thorax, including partial mandible superiorly and upper lung fields inferiorly
Large, well-defined, rounded radiolucent (air-filled) structure overlying the left side of the neck at approximately the C3-C5 level, with sharp margins, situated anterior and lateral to the trachea
The trachea appears midline or minimally displaced to the right at the level of the lucent structure
Cervical vertebral alignment appears grossly intact on this AP view; intervertebral disc spaces appear preserved
Upper lung fields visible at the inferior margin; no obvious gross opacification
Mandible and lower dentition visible superiorly; no gross bony destruction identified
No visible calcification within the lucent cervical mass
Soft tissue of the neck otherwise unremarkable in density aside from the described lucency
differential: Branchial cleft cyst (second branchial cleft cyst with air-fluid level or gas-containing cyst, or fistula tract containing air)
Laryngocele or pharyngocele (air-filled saccular outpouching from the laryngeal ventricle or pharynx)
Abscess with gas formation (infected neck space abscess containing gas, e.g., Ludwig's angina or deep neck space infection with gas-forming organisms)
anatomyConcerns: The radiolucent rounded structure is unusually large and well-defined for normal anatomy; it does not correspond to any normal air-containing structure in this location on a standard AP projection
Slight rotation of the patient cannot be fully excluded, which could affect assessment of tracheal deviation
The field of view clips the skull base superiorly, limiting full craniocervical junction assessment
